items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1965-09-13
items.q: I never did get to know Steve Lewis, who Dr. Souchon tells me was very, very good.

ctx.x: You said before that there were no specific pianists who influenced you when you came up. Generally speaking, what pianists would influence your style, do you think?

Well, I heard pianists all around me, but many of the good pianists, such as Jelly Roll, had already gone. As you say, why did some of these musicians hate to leave? Well, they all hated to leave, I guess, but more or less the musicians who felt that they wanted to make something, or make a name, or make money, they couldn't do it in the Walls. They had to leave. And, of course, Jelly Roll was gone, Spencer Williams was gone, Clarence Williams, King Oliver, all the real greats struck out sooner or later. And…
Well, certainly your piano style goes beyond the ragtime realm. What have any other pianists of the swing era or the modern era influence your playing as it's constituted today?

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1960-07-14
items.q: And of course I had heard of him and heard of Steve Lewis.

ctx.x: How were you when you went to see Mrs. Asset?

I imagine I was about eight or nine years old. I couldn't have been much younger or older than that. And I didn't stay with her too long, about a year maybe a little better. And then I began practicing all these chords and listening to the sounds and getting pointers here and there from different piano players. Of course, I wish I had met Jelly Rule but he had already left. He was a little bit too far before me. And of course I had heard of him and heard of Steve Lewis. I knew, I had heard a lot of good piano…
Oh, about your grandfather, did he play by music or was he a faker or both?

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: Steve Lewis was around here, which was an excellent, excellent black pianist.

ctx.x: And most piano players, I take it around that time, let's say, set in 1915 or 1910 or whatever. You were born in 1910. We're band pianists.

They weren't so pianists. Band pianists, right. And you see, a lot of the good pianists that had kind of left around here by the time that I was coming up. Jelly Roll had been, Jelly Roll was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Tony Jackson was gone. You had many, many, I guess, were still around here. You had many local fellows, local pianists around town. Steve Lewis was around here, which was an excellent, excellent black pianist. Wonderful. And, well, like…
Did they, did the marching bands play Dixieland? Was that a term?
